# The Shape of the Machine

It helps to picture the host, because its shape encodes its decisions. This
is a description, not a procedure — the procedure has its own home, and the
final chapter points to it. What follows is the architecture as an operator
would narrate it while walking a colleague through the rack.

The foundation is Windows Server 2025, chosen not for novelty but for
continuity. The federal customer base already runs Active Directory, the
certificate authority, IIS, and Windows Server at scale, with PowerShell as
its lingua franca and AppLocker and code-integrity tooling already in hand.
A Windows-native authority inherits all of that operator competence
directly, where a Linux alternative would impose a new operational stack on
a substrate the rest of the architecture assumes is Windows-administered.
The host is domain-joined to the legacy forest and registered in the modern
tenant at once — straddling both authorities deliberately, because the
estate it governs straddles them too.

At the edge sits IIS, and IIS alone faces the network. It terminates TLS on
the standard secure port, sets the security headers that a hardened web
front-end is expected to set, and forwards every request inward. Behind it,
reachable only on the loopback interface, runs Gitea — the Git service
proper, with its web interface, its API, its issues and pull requests and
hook machinery. Gitea is never bound to the public interface; the only
process the outside world can reach is the reverse proxy in front of it.
This is a deliberate narrowing: one door, watched, logging every
authenticated principal on every request, feeding the same telemetry
pipeline as everything else in the estate.

Beneath the Git service is its memory. The repositories — the bare object
stores that actually hold canon — live on a dedicated data volume with
tightly scoped permissions, while Gitea's relational state lives in a
PostgreSQL database on a separate host. Secrets are not pasted into config
files; they are drawn from a managed secret store under the service's own
identity. Large binary artifacts have a home too, through the Git LFS server
the service runs natively, so that the corpus can hold weight without
bloating its history.

The most consequential decision is the quietest one: identity. Gitea does
not run as a person and does not run as an all-powerful local account. It
runs as a group-managed service account — a machine identity the directory
itself issues and rotates, with exactly the rights it needs and no more.
Operators, meanwhile, never authenticate to the host as the host; they
authenticate as themselves. Internal staff arrive over secure LDAP against
the forest, mapped to native identities; contributors who live in the modern
tenant arrive over OpenID Connect, their group claims flowing in with them.
The effect is the one the whole series has been building toward: the same
identity that authorizes a read of the forest authorizes a push to canon.
There is no second identity bridge to maintain, no parallel account store to
drift out of sync — the coordinate the enterprise already trusts is the
coordinate that opens the door.

That door, and what it checks before it opens, is where the architecture
finally pays off. The next chapter stands at it.
